summary:
What does it take to design and operate a spacecraft capable of exploring Jupiter? Our game puts players in the role of a systems engineer working alongside the original Galileo mission team.
Players take the role of systems engineers, making decisions about spacecraft architecture, radiation protection, thermal control, power generation, component assembly, and mission planning. They also face real mission challenges, including launch delays, the failure of the high-gain antenna, and the atmospheric probe’s descent.
Our goal is to increase public interest in space exploration and make complex space missions more accessible. That is why we developed the game in three languages: English, Russian, and Kazakh. We also wanted to highlight the people behind major space achievements. Therefore, the game’s characters, events, and technical information are based on the actual history of the Galileo mission. By combining interactive gameplay with historical accuracy, we aim to show not only how space missions work, but also the people and engineering challenges behind them.
details:
Project Details

Our project is an interactive educational game based on NASA’s Galileo mission to Jupiter. Players take on the role of systems engineers working alongside the original mission team, experiencing the main stages of spacecraft design, preparation, and operation.

Gameplay Mechanics

The game guides players through the different stages of developing a space mission. First, they define Galileo’s scientific objectives and choose its architecture, consisting of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. Players then face engineering challenges involving radiation protection, thermal control, power generation, and structural design. They must compare different solutions, consider technical limitations, and make their own engineering decisions.

In a spacecraft assembly mini-game, players explore a hangar, identify essential spacecraft components, and learn their functions. They then plan Galileo’s journey to Jupiter using gravity-assist manoeuvres and navigate the historical launch timeline. Later, players encounter real mission difficulties, including launch delays and the failure of the high-gain antenna, for which they must find alternative communication solutions. Another mini-game focuses on the atmospheric probe's descent, where players must collect scientific measurements about the composition of the gas giant’s atmosphere and transmit data to the orbiter within a limited time.

Advantages and Educational Value

One of our project's main advantages is its accessibility. The game is available in three languages: English, Russian, and Kazakh, allowing us to reach a wider audience. We also prioritised factual accuracy. The technical information, spacecraft components, historical events, mission timeline, and characters are based on the actual Galileo mission.

Expected Impact

Our goal is to increase awareness of the challenges engineers face when developing and operating space missions. We also want to highlight the people behind major scientific achievements, showing that every successful mission involves real specialists, difficult decisions, setbacks, and teamwork. Ultimately, we hope to encourage greater interest in space exploration, engineering, and scientific research.

Development Tools

We used Unity as the main game engine, Blender for creating 3D models, and Procreate for illustrating characters, backgrounds, and other visual elements. Claude was used as an auxiliary tool to accelerate the programming process.

Creativity and Innovation

The main creative aspect of our project is the combination of historical accuracy and interactive engineering simulation. We aimed to recreate not only the successful stages of the Galileo mission but also the real failures and technical difficulties its team encountered. All characters are based on real people involved in the mission, and the events follow its historical chronology.

Unlike traditional educational materials, our game does not simply explain how a space mission works. Instead, it allows players to make engineering decisions themselves. Progress requires analysing technical information, comparing possible solutions, and considering engineering constraints. We also wanted to demonstrate how much research, reading, analysis, and teamwork are involved in developing a real spacecraft. This gives players a better understanding of the engineering process and the people behind major space exploration projects.

Historical Accuracy and Technical Considerations

Several factors were especially important during development. For the gravity-assist simulation, we used the actual planetary positions corresponding to the period between October 12 and November 21. We also considered the historical sequence of mission events and based the game's characters on real members of the Galileo team. At every stage, we tried to balance engaging gameplay with realistic engineering challenges, ensuring that players would need to apply critical thinking rather than simply follow instructions.
